newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: President Ramos says looking into defector case.
newsitem.headline: President Ramos says looking into defector case.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos said on Sunday he was looking into the case of a North Korean defector in China after a top aide said Manila had been asked to take him in transit if he was allowed to go to Seoul.
"I've been hearing it also from the news services," Ramos told Reuters in a brief interview during his visit to the mountain resort city of Baguio in the northern Philippines.
"Our foreign affairs (department) has been tasked to look into the matter to find out (what) this is all about," Ramos added. He declined to answer further questions.

Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said on Saturday the Philippines had been asked to serve as a transit point for Hwang Jang-yop, stranded in the South Korean consular compound in Beijing since February 12, if he was permitted to leave for South Korea.

Siazon indicated Manila was prepared to accept the request in order to help resolve the diplomatic impasse, but stressed there had been no definite word the Philippines would be a stop-off point for any transfer of Hwang to South Korea.
Hwang is the most senior official to defect from North Korea and the two Koreas and China have been discussing his fate.
A Manila diplomatic source said one of the matters under discussion was how long Hwang would remain in the Philippines if he transited through the country.
One suggestion was for him to stay at least one week and up to a month, said one of the sources, who asked not to be identified.
When asked if it was likely Hwang would stay in the Philippines for a few days, a top Foreign Office official said: "Most probably."

"It cannot be that he will not get out of the plane because that would be like going direct from Beijing to Seoul. That would defeat the third country arrangement," said the senior official, who insisted on anonymity.
"The North does not want him to fly direct (to South Korea)," he added. He said it was unclear how strong the possibility was of the Philippines being a transit point.
The official said news of the Philippines' playing a role in solving the impasse was first leaked in South Korea to the Japanese Kyodo news agency.
"It is also possible that we are being used as a decoy," he added.
Siazon told reporters on Saturday before he left on an official visit to Japan that some other routes besides the Philippines were probably being considered.
He said the Philippines wanted to contribute in solving the problem between the two Koreas and China.

"...We are all in Asia -- we don't wish this particular problem to evolve into a more serious politicial difficulty among the three parties, so we would in that context be prepared to make our contribution," Siazon said.
Hwang has said he wants to go to South Korea and foreign diplomats said that he was likely be allowed to leave for a third country first and then travel to Seoul.
